extracted.intended_audience: US patent applicants, inventors, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on when and how to file a Request for Continued Examination (RCE) before the USPTO, including strategic considerations (examiner interviews, after-final responses, IDS timing), costs, and likely outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an RCE is appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE comes into play when dealing with a Final Office Action. An RCE makes sense when an applicant has received a Final Office Action and desires to make further claim amendments and/or arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, if the contemplated claim amendments would require the examiner to perform a further search of the prior art (or at least cause the examiner to feel that way), then an RCE would be suitable. Sometimes, conducting an examiner interview prior to filing a response may be useful in determining whether an RCE is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an RCE is unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all Final Office Actions require an RCE. If the examiner has indicated that certain claims would be allowable, then you may simply file an after-final response taking the allowable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An RCE might also be unnecessary if you are considering only narrowing claim amendments. For example, filing an after-final response with an AFCP request may be an option. It will be up to the Examiner to choose whether they will entertain such an after-final response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of relying on after-final response instead of filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: An after-final response containing more substantial claim amendments or substantive arguments will likely lead to an Advisory Action stating that an RCE should be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an after-final response first may necessitate extension fees if and when the examiner requires an RCE because the response deadline (and need for extensions) will be triggered by the date of the Final Office Action. If the Examiner issues an Advisory Action requiring an RCE, and you file the RCE by the 4-month date from the date of the Final Office Action, you will need to pay a USPTO extension fee for a 1-month extension of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDS filing timing rule that mandates an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Final Office Action is outstanding and an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) must be filed, determine the date the applicant first became aware of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If that earliest date of awareness is less than 3 months from the date the IDS is filed, then the applicant can avoid an RCE and simply pay a nominal USPTO fee ($260/$130 (large/small entity)). If the date the applicant first became aware of the new prior art was more than 3 months from the date of the IDS to be filed, then the applicant must file an RCE in order to submit the IDS.

rubrics_metrics.name: RCE resets the examiner's 'counter' (advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: An RCE resets the counter so that the examiner gets more time to review claim amendments and search the prior art accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due to high caseload, a patent examiner is given a limited allocation of time to review each application and search the relevant prior art. If an applicant’s response to a non-final Office Action doesn’t convince the examiner to allow the case, then the examiner is not getting any further credit by issuing a second non-final action. The system incentives patent examiners to issue final actions; an RCE resets that allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to file an RCE (procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The request itself is a fairly straightforward transmittal form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RCE may be filed with a response or subsequent to the filing of an after-final response. In most cases, you will likely want to file an Office Action response with further claim amendments and arguments in conjunction with the RCE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: As of the date of this post, the small entity USPTO fee is $544 for the first RCE and $800 for the second and subsequent requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should budget these USPTO fees when deciding between filing an RCE, filing additional after-final responses, or pursuing an appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on number of RCEs (practical consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no maximum number of RCEs an applicant may file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a certain point in an application where no further meaningful amendments or arguments can be made, it may make more financial sense to appeal than to file another RCE. If two or more RCEs have already been filed, you may have reached the end of the road with a particular examiner and a patent appeal may make more sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible outcomes after filing an RCE
rubrics_metrics.description: After an RCE is filed, an examiner might allow your patent application. If not, the examiner will issue another Office Action which would typically be non-final, especially if the applicant introduced additional claim amendments and/or new arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant would have the opportunity to respond to this second non-final action. At some point, the applicant may have to make the difficult decision of whether to abandon or continue fighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examiner interviews and strategic amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: With the proper use of examiner interviews and strategic claim amendments and arguments, you might be able to get your patent application allowed without unnecessary filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conducting an examiner interview prior to filing a response may be useful in determining whether an RCE is warranted; strategic claim amendments and arguments may avoid the need for an RCE or increase the chance of allowance after filing one.
